Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Technology Taiwan charges nine people for smuggling ‘high-end’ AI servers to China Among those charged are two Super Micro employees and one from Nvidia, marking another flashpoint in US-China AI rivalry Associated Press Tue 25 Aug 2026 15.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Taiwanese prosecutors charged nine people Monday, including one from Nvidia and two from Super Micro, for illegally exporting “high-end AI servers” to mainland China, adding another wave of turbulence in the AI ​​rivalry between China and the United States. Prosecutors said the servers involved were graphics processing units known as “B300,” which have been banned from sale to China . Seventy-four servers arrived in China successfully, according to the prosecutors. Of those, 50 were sent through Indonesia, 16 delivered directly to China and eight sent to Japan first, then Hong Kong, before they landed in mainland China. Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’ Read more Another attempt involving 56 servers failed, and the servers remain in Taiwan, said the prosecutor’s office. AI infrastructure, including advanced semiconductors mostly made in Taiwan, has become a key point of competition between the US and China. Washington began imposing restrictions on Nvidia’s exports of advanced chips to China in 2022 and tightened them in subsequent years. In April 2025, the US required licenses for exports of Nvidia’s H20 chips to China before allowing some sales to resume later that year. Under export controls, any sale by Nvidia of high-end AI servers – the computer infrastructure that houses the chips needed to power AI systems – requires a strict review process, according to a document from Keelung District prosecutors’ office in Taiwan. The document also said purchases of more than eight high-end AI servers require company staff to conduct on-site checks to the clients. “We will work with the Taiwan authorities to help them resolve the allegations as quickly as possible,” Patrick Rutherford, an Nvidia spokesperson, said in a written statement. Super Micro said in a written statement that the arrests of two of its former employees were due to its cooperation with the Taiwanese authorities and the company will continue to work to “enhance its robust export compliance program to protect American innovation”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion Prosecutors are seeking the maximum five-year sentences for four of the nine defendants, including Chang, an Nvidia manager identified just by his family name. Chang was the “key figure” responsible for “authorizing the release of the B300 GPUs” in this case but “demonstrated a clearly poor attitude following the offense”, the document said. Some of the defendants set up a company in Japan, which helped successfully transfer eight of the servers, prosecutors said. Some allegedly created fake websites and falsified information to evade export restrictions. https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text: One teacher said: ‘If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school.’ Photograph: redsnapper/Alamy View image in fullscreen One teacher said: ‘If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school.’ Photograph: redsnapper/Alamy School attendance and absence Teachers say holidays in term can be worth more than time in school School staff tell focus groups they believe school system in England and Wales cannot deal with attendance crisis Alexandra Topping Political correspondent Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Teachers have so little belief in the importance of pupils’ full school attendance that they would take their own children on term time holidays if they could, staff have told a three-year research programme. Frontline staff do not believe the school system is set up to deal with an ongoing attendance crisis in England and Wales, where nearly one in five children are now missing at least 10% of school, according to a report based on in-depth conversations with teachers. Despite a hardline approach from schools to tackle the crisis, evidence from focus groups containing teachers from schools in low-income areas suggests many share the same scepticism as parents and pupils about the efficiency of holiday fines , according to the report by youth charity Impetus and policy and polling research firm Public First . “If I wasn’t a teacher, I would take my daughter out of school and take her on holiday because it would be cheaper,” said one teacher. Another noted: “If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school in January.” The report comes as the children’s commissioner warned of tens of thousands of hidden Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), with analysis suggesting that an estimated 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds enrolled in colleges in England are attending less than half the time. Rachel de Souza warned that the number of Neets is almost twice as large as official figures indicate, according to a new analysis of 262 of England’s 290 college groups, which are not included in Department for Education attendance figures. ‘Cheap travel is not a defence’: the parents facing court for school absences in England Read more “We have a blind spot: hidden Neets slipping through the cracks,” she said. “Young people with all the negative impacts of not being in employment, education or training, but with none of the targeted interventions.” Researchers compiling the report, A Crisis of Disengagement, spoke to 62 secondary school staff from schools where more than 25% of pupils were eligible for free school meals. They spoke of the work of chasing pupils’ attendance as “relentless” and expressed the view that an occasional holiday or minor absence was less worrying than sustained disengagement. While some staff saw fines as a necessary tool, many believed they damage trust and undermine the relational work needed to support pupils and families to re-engage with school. “We’ll send a penalty notice out and then we’ve really annoyed that parent,” said one senior leader. “We’ve just broken a relationship between a family that we want to get into school.” A record 492,825 penalty notices for unauthorised absences were issued to parents in England in 2024-25, a sharp rise from pre-Covid levels. Researchers have previously warned of a “seismic shift” in attitudes to attendance since the pandemic, with concern that some parents no longer believe children needed to be in school full-time. The absence rate for pupils in England in 2025-26 was 6.93%, significantly above the 2018-19 pre-Covid level of 4.7% Teachers and senior leaders in schools also argued that gaps in mental health support for struggling students, unmet special educational needs and a paucity of social workers was making their jobs more difficult with schools seen as “the one-stop shop for everything”. “We’ve got children who should have specialist provision, and they’re in our building every day,” said one senior leader. “We also need external agencies such as CAMHS [Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services] and social workers to have the right capacity and not turn us down.” Staff also told researchers the most effective interventions were also the hardest – including building relationships, mentoring and home visits. “I think it takes up a lot of adult hours,” she said. “If you looked proportionally at how time was broken down, attendance is very, very time consuming.” Susannah Hardyman, CEO of Impetus, said teachers could not solve the attendance crisis alone. “We now know that not only are pupils, families and teachers unconvinced that every day in school matters, but what we are facing is a wider crisis of disengagement driven by pressures often outside the control of school staff,” she said. http://www.journalreview.com/stories/pre.text: President Trump intensifies war on American press NOBLESVILLE — Our caravan of almost two dozen refurbished Indiana ambulances and fire trucks snaked into Guatemala City after sunset in November 1988. Earlier that day, we had met in the border town of Tapachula with a squadron of bomberos, who greeted us by ripping their department patches off their uniform sleeves as a gift. When we arrived in the capital, several dozen Hoosier Lions Club members stared, transfixed, at glowing streams of lava coursing down the sides of a volcano looming in the distance. It was a fascinating entry into this Central American nation that was attempting to break the grip of authoritarian rule over the previous three years after four decades of civil war that had claimed 250,000 lives. A new constitution followed a series of coups; Marco Vinicio Cerezo Arévalo was the first civilian president in decades, but the civil war and remnants of iron rule still festered. The next morning, a different reality settled in. At about every other intersection in the capital’s downtown, a jeep sat with two or three soldiers. It was a not-so-subtle show of banana republic force. In my American experience, such a display of military power came after civil unrest, followed by a governor calling up the National Guard. Later that day, the clerk at our hotel warned me about the sprawling national security facility just around the corner. “If you take a picture of it, somebody will come out and smash your camera,” the clerk said. “Or, perhaps, take you inside.” I took his advice seriously. In my four decades as a professional journalist, this was the first of three times I grappled with an authoritarian regime. The second came in 2007 when I joined a congressional delegation headed by U.S. Sen. Richard Lugar and former colleague Sam Nunn. Destination: Moscow, less than a decade after strongman President Vladimir Putin emerged. Russia had evolved from a Communist Soviet state with totalitarian rule before it fractured into 15 republics in 1991. After tormented democratic and capitalist impulses were shattered under the rule of Boris Yeltsin, he handpicked Putin, the former KGB agent who eventually displaced liberal rule for an authoritarian state. It is now morphing into a totalitarian retrenchment since his 2022 war with Ukraine commenced. The Lugar delegation was situated at the Grand Moscow Marriott. For the first several days, a series of Carnegie Moscow Center seminars took place. After returning to my hotel room from one such event, I found it in disarray. My papers had been scattered about the room. My luggage had been searched. I reported the incident to Andy Fisher, Lugar’s communications director, who was not surprised. Previous Lugar codels had found agents standing for long periods outside hotel rooms. Everyone assumed the phones and rooms were bugged. As the Lugar-Nunn codel prepared to leave Yekaterinburg, Russia, for Odesa, Ukraine, I was told my passport was missing. I had given it to U.S. Navy Chief Floyd Logan, who managed codel personnel and kept all our passports. The situation set off a flurry of phone calls among American diplomats. About 15 minutes later, my passport turned up. I hustled to the plane, which took off just minutes later. Once in the air, I turned to Kenneth Myers III, a Pentagon nuclear deterrence official. “What the hell was that about?” I asked. “They didn’t know who you were,” he said. “They just wanted to take one last look at you.” I relate these experiences while my country — the United States of America — appears to be sliding into an authoritarian state, with the First Amendment on the line. President Donald J. Trump has branded American journalists with the Stalinist phrase “enemies of the state.” There have been lawsuits against The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, ABC News and CBS’s “60 Minutes.” ABC and CBS settled for millions. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has booted mainstream news organizations from the Pentagon while he purges 20 generals and admirals and is now directing a war against Iran, with little official information. Unlike other conflicts, there are no reporters embedded with our troops. Late-night comedians such as Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel have faced scrutiny from Trump’s Federal Communications Commission over … jokes. Trump attempted to bar The Associated Press from the White House after it refused to call the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” This past Friday, Trump announced on Truth Social that he is banning CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House. Trump complained that “something is wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories.” Federal Judge Timothy Kelly — a Trump appointee — ordered access restored, which the White House defied until mid-day Thursday. For several hours, Chinese state media had access to the White House; American reporters did not. On Monday, he debuted Trump TV on YouTube, borrowing a page from Indiana Gov. Mike Pence, who in January 2015 scuttled plans for Just IN, a government-run news service intended to bypass the press after it ignited fierce criticism. Trump appears to be seeking to reinforce his rule in the court of public opinion rather than the rule of law. And like Putin, Hungary’s former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, these regimes attempt to co-opt existing media, as mogul David Ellison has done to CBS News and now CNN. Reporters Without Borders, a free press organization based in Paris, counts 130 journalists jailed in Turkey. Orbán created what the Los Angeles Times described as “an almost Orwellian environment” where the government weaponized its control of a majority of news outlets. Putin has ordered the murder of 43 reporters since 1999. A Sept. 15 Pew Research Center poll revealed 73% of Americans (including 66% of Republicans and 81% of Democrats) believe press freedom is extremely important to society’s well-being. In “The Prevention of Literature,” English author George Orwell wrote, “Freedom of the press, if it means anything at all, means the freedom to criticize and oppose.” That was the crux of what sent colonial aristocrats into a revolutionary mode 250 years ago. But Orwell also warned, “Unpopular ideas can be silenced, and inconvenient facts kept dark, without the need for any official ban.” Brian A. Howey is an opinion columnist for State Affairs Indiana and the founder of Howey Politics Indiana. His writing offers analysis and opinion shaped by decades of experience covering Indiana politics. Email him at howey@stateaffairs.com. https://www.bursa.ro/the-muresan-cabinet.text: Designated Prime Minister Siegfried Mureşan and his team of ministers will appear before the plenary session of Parliament today to present the government program and seek a vote of investiture from the senators and deputies. Under the Constitution, the government lineup proposed by Siegfried Mureşan requires the support of half plus one of the total number of senators and deputies-meaning 233 votes in favor out of 465 parliamentarians. According to statements made yesterday by Csoma Botond, leader of the UDMR deputies, the PNL-USR-UDMR coalition did not have the necessary votes to confirm the Mureşan government as of last night. This is also confirmed by designated Prime Minister Siegfried Mureşan, who announced yesterday morning that he still needed 33 to 40 votes to secure parliamentary approval. What is certain is that today will see a heated parliamentary session, much like yesterday's proceedings in the specialized committees-the second day of hearings for the ministers proposed by Siegfried Mureşan, some of whom received favorable opinions while the majority received negative ones. Among those who received a favorable opinion yesterday is Mircea Abrudean, President of the Senate and candidate for the position of Minister of Internal Affairs in the Mureşan Cabinet. Among Mircea Abrudean's priorities for the Ministry of Internal Affairs are securing borders, protecting citizens, strengthening Romania's capacity to respond to new security threats, combating domestic violence and femicide, and fighting drug trafficking. Mircea Abrudean stated: "The Ministry of Internal Affairs is part of Romania's national security architecture, and its institutions must be prepared for risks that have evolved significantly in recent years. Cross-border crime, hybrid threats, and risks to critical infrastructure can rapidly shift from the realm of public order to that of national security. Furthermore, the changing security landscape in the Black Sea region necessitates the development of surveillance capabilities for both maritime borders and critical infrastructure. At the same time, security begins with the protection of people. I envision a state that protects its citizens when they need it. We must rebuild trust in the Romanian Police and place the protection of life and citizen safety at the heart of the Ministry's activities." The second minister to receive a favorable recommendation was Dragoş Pîslaru, the nominee for the position of Minister of Investments and European Projects-a role he currently holds. Addressing the specialized committees, Dragoş Pîslaru stated that, over the past 12 months, Romania has secured 10 billion euros in European funds (8 billion from cohesion funds and 2.5 billion from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan), marking an unprecedented achievement. Raluca Turcan, the nominee for Minister of Labor, Family, Youth, and Social Solidarity, received a negative opinion from the members of the relevant parliamentary committees. Her hearing was marked by several incidents, including having her microphone cut off just as she was presenting her proposal regarding service pensions. "You have already exceeded the initially agreed time by six minutes (...) Thank you; you spoke very eloquently and well. We are convinced that all these recurring issues you bring up every four years will ultimately be resolved-as always-by a Constitutional Court ruling declaring them unconstitutional," said the session chair, Adrian Solomon (PSD). Regarding service pensions, Turcan stated: "When it comes to service pensions, there is an anomaly not found in other countries: having people at the prime age for the labor market retire and then immediately get rehired the very next moment (...) That is why the bill currently in Parliament-aimed at reconciling service pensions with salary income-is an initiative I urge us all to support, as it would add 1.5 billion lei to the state budget." Other measures announced by Raluca Turcan include eliminating the excessive taxation of part-time contracts in the healthcare and education sectors, as well as for families with children and young people classified as NEETs (Not in Education, Employment, or Training). Oana Gheorghiu, the nominee for Minister of Health, also received a negative opinion. This also drew a reaction from Prime Minister-designate Siegfried Mureşan: "Oana Gheorghiu, who built a hospital from scratch starting with a budget of zero lei, received a negative opinion as Minister of Health from the PSD members who haven't built a single hospital, even though they had the entire national budget at their disposal." He went on to note that this amounted to "a vote rejecting competence and values." The hearing of the current Deputy Prime Minister in charge of state-owned enterprise reform was tense, as former Health Ministers-Social Democrats Alexandru Rafila and Alexandru Rogobete-accused her of lacking the competence for the role, which she herself likened to managing an non-governmental organizations. Oana Gheorghiu was actually interrupted several times by PSD representatives while answering questions. One of the nominees who received a surprisingly favorable endorsement is Oana Ţoiu, the candidate for Minister of Foreign Affairs. Ţoiu, who has served as Foreign Minister in the Bolojan cabinet for over fifteen months, stated during the hearings that she aims to "continue" the course she has already set. "Our main objectives are very clear: strengthening security and ensuring the safety of Romanian citizens are our primary goals, given that we are the EU state sharing the longest border with the war [in Ukraine - Ed.]," she stated. According to the USR nominee, Romania will focus on strengthening its partnership with the USA, "which rests on two pillars: security and investment." Oana Ţoiu also told lawmakers that Romania has the "power and the right" to participate in any international negotiation. "Regarding representation, I want to highlight a crucial principle that must be an imperative for Romania's foreign policy: the capacity, right, and power Romania has secured to pursue the national interest in any international negotiation... Romania has earned the right to sit at the table of any negotiation," she asserted. According to the nominee for Foreign Minister, the institution requires reinforcement in terms of both personnel and state budget funding. Ţoiu pointed out that "35% of foreign service staff positions are unfilled" and that "99% of the funds allocated for human resources" within the ministry have already been spent. Social Democrat Florin Manole asked Oana Ţoiu whether it was justifiable for the Romanian state to pay $21,000 in monthly rent for the luxury villa housing Romania's ambassador to Washington, Andrei Muraru. Oana Ţoiu replied that the contract in question had been extended during the tenures of Prime Minister Marcel Ciolacu, a fellow party member of Florin Manole. Andrea Chiş-nominated for Minister of Justice, a former judge at the Cluj Court of Appeal and former member of the Superior Council of Magistracy-received an unfavorable opinion from the specialized committees of the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. When asked about the amount of the pension she currently receives and about the special pensions for magistrates, Andreea Chiş said: "My pension is currently 40,000 lei. I did not set it myself. Regarding the amount, I have maintained that a pension should not exceed one's salary. I warned as early as 2018 that a wave of retirements would follow, precisely because there was pressure within the system; judges felt this pressure and were offered the chance to leave honorably and enjoy an easier life. (...) My position has been consistent-though it was not adopted-and the pension amount does not depend on me. It seems unfair for there to be a discrepancy between pensions already being paid and those of people retiring later. (...) It might be considered unfair, but if we acknowledge that something was done wrong at some point-or if society perceives it that way, regardless of what we magistrates might want-it is important to realize that we cannot perpetuate a situation indefinitely simply because it happened once. Whether or not it is possible to reduce pensions currently in payment depends on the Constitutional Court, which has already issued a ruling. It is not something that depends on me. Speaking personally, it was not the money that drove me to become a judge, to seek promotion to a specific court, or to serve as a member of the CSM." Another favorable opinion was issued for Bulcsu Koppany Otvos, the UDMR candidate for the position of Minister of Culture. The final ministers to undergo hearings last night were Mihai Dimian-nominated as Minister of Education and Research-Cseke Attila-nominated as Minister of Development, Public Works, and Administration-and Diana Buzoianu-nominated as Minister of Environment, Waters, and Forests. Today, all the aforementioned individuals, together with Prime Minister Siegfried Mureşan and their colleagues who were heard by parliamentary committees on Monday, will await the investiture vote in the plenary session of Parliament. Articol despre Siegfried Muresan, government, investiture, Parliament, ministerial hearings, Andrea Chis, Mircea Abrudean.
